scenes.recognized_speech: Imagine sliding the top corner of a triangular sail sideways along a horizontal rail. The sail can look taller or more slanted. Can its area change while the base and the rail stay fixed?

The base is 6 cm long, the rail is 4 cm above it, measured at a right angle, half of 6 times 4 is 12. The sloping side grows as the peg travels, but the perpendicular height stays 4 even beyond the end of the base.

A triangular field has a fence 9 metres long along its base. A gate splits the fence into lengths 4 and 5. Paths from the opposite corner divide the field into two triangles. The whole field is 36 square metres. Find the area beside the longer fence.

Both triangles reach the same perpendicular height, their areas are in the ratio 4 to 5. 9 equal parts share 36 square meters, so each part is 4, the longer fence belongs to 5 parts, or 20 square meters.

A rectangle is 12 meters wide and 8 meters high, pick any point inside it and draw a line to each corner. The triangle along the bottom has an area of 18 square meters. What is the area of the triangle along the top?
The top and bottom triangles each use a base of 12. Their two perpendicular heights add to 8, however far sideways the point moves. Together their areas are half of 12 times 8 or 48 square meters.
Subtract the bottom area of 18. The top area is 30. To check, the bottom height must be 3 meters, since half of 12 times 3 is 18. The height left for the top is 5, giving 30 again.

Mark the base and draw the height at a right angle, extending the baseline when necessary. Triangles with a shared height divide area in the ratio of their bases. Equal parallel bases can be paired by adding their heights. States.

captions.text: Imagine sliding the top corner of a triangular sail
sideways along a horizontal rail.
The sail can look taller or more slanted.
Can its area change while the base and the
rail stay fixed?
The base is six centimetres long.
The rail is four centimetres above it,
measured at a right angle.
Half of six times four is twelve.
The sloping side grows as the peg travels,
but the perpendicular height stays four, even beyond the
end of the base.
A triangular field has a fence nine metres long
along its base.
A gate splits the fence into lengths four and five.
Paths from the opposite corner divide the field
into two triangles.
The whole field is thirty six square metres.
Find the area beside the longer fence.
Both triangles reach the same perpendicular height.
Their areas are in the ratio four to five.
Nine equal parts share thirty six square metres,
so each part is four.
The longer fence belongs to five parts,
or twenty square metres.
A rectangle is twelve metres wide and eight metres high.
Pick any point inside it and draw a line to each corner.
The triangle along the bottom has an area of
eighteen square metres.
What is the area of the triangle along the top?
The top and bottom triangles each use a base of twelve.
Their two perpendicular heights add to eight,
however far sideways the point moves.
Together their areas are half of twelve times eight,
or forty eight square metres.
Subtract the bottom area of eighteen.
The top area is thirty.
To check, the bottom height must be three metres,
since half of twelve times three is eighteen.
The height left for the top is five,
giving thirty again.
Mark the base and draw the height at a right angle,
extending the base line when necessary.
Triangles with a shared height divide area in the ratio
of their bases.
Equal parallel bases can be paired by
adding their heights.
